title.en: The mountain that became a bridge

text.en: The steel in a railway bridge began as red-brown rock dug out of a hill in Jharkhand or Odisha. That rock is iron ore, and it is one of the minerals that quietly build a modern country. In this lesson we learn what a resource is, what a mineral is, and where India's important minerals are found.

A natural resource is any matter or energy from the environment that living things use, such as air, water, soil, minerals, fossil fuels, plants and wildlife.
Resources are renewable if they regenerate naturally after use, like solar, wind, biogas, tidal and wave energy, and non-renewable if they cannot be replaced after use, like coal, petroleum and natural gas.
A mineral is a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with a definite chemical composition and physical properties, and taking it out of the earth is called mining.
Mines near the surface are open pit mines, while deep mines are called shaft mines.
Four bodies look after minerals in India: the Geological Survey of India at Kolkata, the Indian Bureau of Mines at Nagpur, the Non-Ferrous Materials Technology Development Centre at Hyderabad, and the Ministry of Mines, which administers the Mines and Minerals Act of 1957.
On the basis of their chemical and physical properties, minerals are grouped as metallic minerals, which contain one or more metals, and non-metallic minerals, which contain no metal.
Iron ore is the most important mineral for making iron and steel, and it occurs as magnetite with 72.4 percent iron, hematite 69.9, goethite 62.9, limonite 55 and siderite 48.2.
Jharkhand leads iron ore production with about 25 percent, then Odisha with 21 percent, Karnataka with 20 percent and Chhattisgarh with 18 percent, while Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu give about 5 percent each.
In Tamil Nadu iron ore is notable in Salem, Namakkal, Tiruvannamalai, Tiruchirappalli, Coimbatore, Madurai and Tirunelveli districts, and the Ministry of Steel plans the iron and steel industry through SAIL.
Manganese is a hard, brittle silvery-grey element always found with iron, and nearly 10 kg of it is needed for every tonne of steel, apart from its use in bleaching powder, insecticides, paints and batteries.
The largest manganese deposits are in Odisha, India is the fifth largest producer in the world, and MOIL at Nagpur is the state-owned manganese mining company.
Copper was the first metal used by prehistoric people, it is flexible, it gives brass with zinc and bronze with tin, and it is used for wires, cables and electrical machinery, with Rajasthan holding the largest reserves, then Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh.
Bauxite is the ore of aluminium, found as surface deposits in laterite areas, and light, tough aluminium is used for aircraft and automobile engines, while bauxite also goes into cement and chemicals; the main deposits are in Odisha, and NALCO has units at Angul and Damanjodi.
Non-metallic minerals include mica, limestone, gypsum, nitrate, potash and dolomite, and even coal and petroleum are counted here.
Mica, called abhrak, splits into thin clear sheets and does not conduct electricity yet withstands high voltage, so it is used in electrical goods, and it is found in Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Odisha and Jharkhand.
Limestone is calcium carbonate used for soda ash, caustic soda, paper, cement, iron and steel, glass and fertilisers, and gypsum, a hydrated calcium sulphate, is used for cement, fertilisers, wall board, plaster of Paris and soil conditioning.

problem.en: A steel mill melts 10 tonnes of magnetite ore. How much iron can it contain, and would siderite of the same weight give more or less?

text.en: Magnetite has 72.4 percent iron, so 10 tonnes contain 10 x 72.4 / 100 = 7.24 tonnes of iron.

why.en: Iron content is the percentage multiplied by the weight.

text.en: Siderite has only 48.2 percent iron, so 10 tonnes contain 4.82 tonnes.

why.en: Same method with the lower percentage.

text.en: So siderite gives 2.42 tonnes less iron than magnetite for the same weight.

why.en: 7.24 minus 4.82 is 2.42, which is why magnetite is the richest ore.

prompt.en: Explain to a friend the difference between metallic and non-metallic minerals and give two examples of each with one use.

requiredIdeas.en: Metallic minerals contain metals, for example iron ore for steel and bauxite for aluminium
Non-metallic minerals contain no metal, for example mica for electrical goods and limestone for cement
Iron ore leading states are Jharkhand and Odisha

commonMisconceptions.en: Mica conducts electricity (it does not, it insulates)
Bauxite is an ore of copper (it is the ore of aluminium)

points.en: A resource is renewable if it regenerates naturally and non-renewable if it cannot be replaced.
Metallic minerals: iron, manganese, copper, bauxite. Non-metallic: mica, limestone, gypsum.
Magnetite has the most iron (72.4%); Jharkhand leads iron ore output, then Odisha.
Manganese is needed for steel (about 10 kg per tonne); bauxite gives aluminium; mica insulates; limestone and gypsum go into cement.
